title: The Remnant and the Stone of Stumbling
english: …he drove so far into wicked ways as to be from then on a vessel of wrath and of destruction. God made use of this man to display the strength that is in himself, so that his name might be proclaimed in all the earth (Romans 9:17), and so that Pharaoh, when he suffered, might be seen to deserve his suffering; for suffering was owed to him for his first sins, even if he had not offended by his later ones. So let every reproach and every idle charge against God be dismissed. For “desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, he endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction” (Romans 9:22), in order to benefit vessels of mercy (Romans 9:23), that is, those who have received mercy through faith; for we have been called not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles (Romans 9:24).

“As indeed he says in Hosea” (Romans 9:25). We too, the servants of idols, who did not know the one who is God by nature and in truth, were not his people (Hosea 2:23); but we have received mercy through faith, have come under him, have been called through grace, and have been justified and sanctified through Christ.

“Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea” (Romans 9:27). So even if Israel were as many as the sand, “the remnant will be saved” (Romans 9:27; Isaiah 10:22), that is, those who have been justified through faith in Christ; and this has come about because God had mercy on them. “For he is completing and cutting short the word” (Romans 9:28). He saved, he says, by “completing and cutting short the word”; that is, he declared to us the preaching of the gospel as an apt and concise and, so to speak, cut-short saying. For the law and the prophets, by a long circuit of words, scarcely set before us through the letter the meaning of what they say; but the preaching of the gospel is simple and a word cut short.

“But Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness” (Romans 9:31). In giving the reasons why not all the Jews have been saved, he at once weaves wonder into his argument and says: What a strange thing! The crowd of those who had gone astray, with no aim at all of doing good, has been justified (Romans 9:30), while Israel, though trained toward righteousness by the law given through Moses, missed its hope and has had no share in the gift that leads to it (Romans 9:31). What the cause is, then, is plain: they did not accept salvation through faith and justification in Christ, but thought that the boasts they had, as in shadows, were enough for them (Romans 9:32).

“A stone of stumbling” (Romans 9:33). Surely we do not say that Christ was set in Israel for this purpose; but since this was foreknown to God, he of necessity foretold what was to be: that a cause of slipping would lie in the foundations of Zion, and that some of the foolish would fall upon it and suffer this from their disobedience (Isaiah 8:14; Isaiah 28:16). He made the prediction for their benefit, not that they should stumble, but that, knowing it beforehand, they might rise above the evil. So Christ has been laid as a precious stone (Isaiah 28:16); but for those who stumble out of unbelief the loss was ruin, while for those who have believed the gain is life and justification.

“For I bear them witness” (Romans 10:2). He bears them witness, then, to their zeal for God; yet he convicts them of having gone astray, because, when they ought to have marvelled at Christ, from the works he was doing, as being by nature…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).
Section opens mid-sentence, completing τουτέστιν εἰς from the close of u09-open; rendered with a leading ellipsis.
τῆς ἐνούσης ἰσχύος αὐτῷ: 'the strength that is in him', i.e. in God, the subject of προσεχρήσατο.

διὰ πρώτας ἁμαρτίας… διὰ τῶν δευτέρων: Pharaoh's earlier sins (idolatry, oppression of Israel, named in u09-open) already deserved punishment, apart from his later resistance; rendered 'first sins… later ones'.
μῶμος καὶ φλυαρία: 'reproach and idle charge'.

Ἔσωσε δέ φησιν λόγον συντελῶν καὶ συντέμνων: Cyril's gloss on the lemma, with ἔσωσε ('he saved') and no object; rendered 'He saved, he says, by “completing and cutting short the word”'. Nothing supplied as object.
λόγιον… συντετμημένον: 'cut-short saying' (λόγιον can mean an oracle); kept close to the lemma's συντέμνων.
Ὢ παραδόξου πράγματος: Cyril's own exclamation, put as Paul's sense ('and says'); not marked as quotation because it is not Paul's wording.
τὰ ὡς ἐν σκιαῖς αὐχήματα: 'the boasts they had, as in shadows', i.e. privileges of the law, which Cyril calls a shadow.
ἀμείνους γένοιντο τοῦ κακοῦ: 'might rise above the evil' (lit. 'become better than the evil').
οὐκ ἦμεν… ἀλλ' ἠλεήθημεν… δεδικαιώμεθά τε καὶ ἡγιάσμεθα may also echo 1 Corinthians 6:11 (ἡγιάσθητε, ἐδικαιώθητε); possible allusion only, so not cited inline.
Page numbers 233, 234 and 235 and the footer numeral '25' are edition apparatus and are omitted.
Section ends mid-sentence at ὡς φύσει; the next row opens with Θεόν. The English keeps the cut at 'as being by nature…'; u09-rem-mid resumes with '…God'.

title: Christ the End of the Law
english: …God, they said instead, “It is not for a good work that we stone you, but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God” (John 10:33). Or it may be read in this way: they have not known the righteousness that comes from God (Romans 10:3), that is, Christ, or else the righteousness that comes through faith in him. Supposing that they were fighting side by side with the law given through Moses, they remained disobedient, not seeking the Son who is able to set free (John 8:36), who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), and who, in his saving dispensation, cuts short the righteousness of the law, so hard to achieve, to give release from hardship and toil.

“For Christ is the end of the law” (Romans 10:4). The law, then, was brought in beforehand to be a tutor for the people of old, leading them to the mystery of Christ (Galatians 3:24), and to give them glimpses of the truth through riddles. That is how we define Christ as the fulfilment of the law and the prophets, and quite rightly. Or would not the truth reasonably be understood to be the fulfilment of every obscure riddle? And how could anyone doubt it? So the passage from what was in shadows to the truth does not do away with the laws given through Moses; rather, it makes their meaning clearer.

Now that things have passed over into truth, and what was in types and riddles has been changed for the better, we do not say that the law has been abolished, but rather that it has been brought to completion at the time when the truth, that is, Christ, shone upon us. For Christ is the end of the law and the prophets, and he would not speak falsely when he says, “I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it” (Matthew 5:17). For just as the many colours, added in due time, by no means do away with the shadowy outlines first sketched on painted panels, but rather bring them into clearer view, in the same way we say that the shadows of the law have not been overturned, but rather brought to completion, as in an advance toward the truth.

“For Moses writes of the righteousness that is from the law,” and the rest (Romans 10:5). “For Moses writes,” he says, “of the righteousness that is from the law, that the person who does it shall live by it” (Romans 10:5; Leviticus 18:5). But there was no one at all who could carry it out blamelessly; for “who will understand transgressions?” (Psalm 19:12). So the grace that justifies is better, and it frees us from the indictment that stands in the law.

“But the righteousness that is from faith speaks thus” (Romans 10:6). He usefully lays down how faith should be practised on our part, if it is to be blameless before God and to seem very well done indeed. For to doubt at all, and to be given to being tossed about into feeble double-mindedness, is utterly to be rejected; and it is perhaps superfluous, and among the most dangerous things of all, to think one must pry into what lies beyond all reason and above our understanding. For how could the things God works in ways beyond words be plain to see? And what eye of the heart could be so great as to be able to behold God? Or rather, who will understand, even if someone chose to speak and set out things that are very far above us? For…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

Section opens mid-sentence: Θεόν completes ὡς φύσει at the close of u09-rem-early; rendered '…God' with a leading ellipsis. οἱ δὲ ἔλεγον: δέ marks the contrast with what they ought to have done, so 'they said instead'.
ἢ οὕτως: Cyril offers a second reading of Romans 10:2–3; rendered 'Or it may be read in this way'.
τουτέστι Χριστόν, ἤτοι τὴν διὰ πίστεως τὴν εἰς αὐτόν: two glosses of 'the righteousness from God'; ἤτοι rendered 'or else'.
συνασπίζειν (lit. 'to stand shield to shield with'): 'fighting side by side with'.

οἰκονομικῶς συστέλλοντα: 'in his saving dispensation, cuts short'; συστέλλω is 'contract, abridge', in line with the 'word cut short' of Romans 9:28 in u09-rem-early. ἵνα δυσχερείας ἀπαλλάξῃ καὶ τριβῆς has no stated object; rendered 'to give release from hardship and toil', nothing supplied.

οὐκοῦν ἀναίρεσιν… ποιεῖται… ἀλλ' ἐκφανεστέραν… καθίστησι: the ἀλλ' requires a negative, so read οὔκουν ('not, then'): the passage to truth does not abolish the laws but makes their meaning clearer. This matches the next sentences (οὐ καταλελύσθαι, οὐκ ἀνατετράφθαι).
ἐκπεπεράνθαι: 'brought to completion' (lit. 'carried through to the end'), Cyril's sense of τέλος here; not 'ended' in the sense of abolished.
The painter image: σκιαί are the preliminary shadow-outlines on a panel (πίναξ), later filled with colour; rendered 'shadowy outlines first sketched on painted panels'.
γραφῆς… τῆς ἐν νόμῳ: legal sense 'indictment', as in u08-rem-close; Colossians 2:14 (χειρόγραφον… τοῖς δόγμασιν) is a possible echo, not cited.
ὁ ποιήσας ἄνθρωπος: 'the person who does it', since ἄνθρωπος here is generic.

διψυχία and καταδονεῖσθαι may echo James 1:6–8 (δίψυχος, a wave tossed); possible allusion only, not cited. καρδίας ὀφθαλμός may echo Ephesians 1:18; possible only, not cited. 'Who will understand' (τίς ἄρα συνήσει) echoes the Psalm verse just quoted.
Page number 236 and the footer numeral '26' are edition apparatus and are omitted.
Section ends mid-sentence at ὁ μὲν γάρ ('For…'); u09-rem-close resumes '…our Lord Jesus Christ once set before Nicodemus…'.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos u09 rem mid

title: Faith, and Israel Not Cast Off
english: …our Lord Jesus Christ once set before Nicodemus the words about spiritual rebirth, and he said, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born from above, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:3, 5). [Then he added to these the words that follow.] But when Nicodemus understood nothing at all, then indeed Christ, showing how far the dullness of the human mind stands from the fineness of these thoughts, says, “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John 3:12). And to these he added, “Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know and bear witness to what we have seen, and no one receives our testimony” (John 3:11).

So the things that are beyond us are not to be put to the test. For if it is true that “we find with difficulty the things that are in our hands,” as it is written (Wisdom of Solomon 9:16), how can we not see that, in matters beyond reason at least, faith is of the greatest use, with no inquiry following after it and no idle questioning brought to bear? For it is by understanding that matters of this kind are splendidly honoured.

“Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (Romans 10:11), and the rest. Let Israel not make salvation through faith its own private good. For, he says, “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13), whether he is a Jew or a Greek, a slave or free. The God of all saves without distinction, for all things are his. In this sense we say that all things are summed up in Christ (Ephesians 1:10).

“Has God rejected his people? By no means” (Romans 11:1). Paul acts wisely. Although Israel had suffered the darkening, he does not let it be hardened still further by utter despair, but he goes after it, as it were, with skill and with kind words. For just now he was accusing Israel of disobedience; yet he does not strip it of the hope that comes from above, nor does he say that it has been wholly thrust out of its closeness to God.

And he makes the proof of the matter plain by setting himself forward as an Israelite and of the seed of Abraham (Romans 11:1). Most aptly, too, he still calls them God’s people, and he adds “By no means” to the words about being rejected. This was the act of one who, as it were, gently wins over those who had chosen to disobey, coming round them with coaxing words and bringing them to a devout and teachable habit of mind. If, then, it is evident that he himself has been called to apostleship, and has been appointed a minister of the sacred mysteries of the Saviour, a herald and apostle to the nations (1 Timothy 2:7), although he is from Israel, it is plain that “God has not rejected his people” (Romans 11:2).

“Or do you not know what the Scripture says in the story of Elijah?” (Romans 11:2). Most fittingly he brings in the account of Elijah as a kind of picture of what had happened to Israel. For from the likeness of the events of that time one can easily see that Israel itself has acted outrageously, to its own harm. When Ahab reigned over Samaria, things carved by hand were worshipped by Israel beyond all bounds, and there were sacrifices and sacred precincts everywhere (1 Kings 16:29–33). Those who held fast to God were utterly afraid, and so hard to bear…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: ὁ μὲν γὰρ ('For ...') stands at the end of u09-rem-mid; the leading ellipsis marks the join.

Ends mid-sentence at καὶ δύσοιστον, which governs τὴν δίωξιν in u10-open (δύσοιστον οὕτω τὴν δίωξιν ὑπομεμενήκασιν, ὡς…: 'so hard to bear was the persecution they endured that…'). Rendered 'and so hard to bear…'; u10-open resumes '…was the persecution they endured that…'. Nothing supplied.
The bracketed clause [εἶτα τούτοις προσετίθει τὰ ἐφεξῆς] is bracketed in the copy-text and kept in brackets.
PG column numbers 237 and 238 and the page number 27 in the copy-text are dropped from the reading text.
συνιέντος δὲ αὐτοῦ: the subject is Nicodemus; named in English for clarity.

τῆς τῶν ἐννοιῶν ἰσχνότητος ὡς ἀπωτάτω τιθεὶς τῆς ἀνθρώπου διανοίας τὸ πάχος: literally 'placing the thickness of human understanding as far as possible from the fineness of the concepts'; rendered 'showing how far the dullness of the human mind stands from the fineness of these thoughts'.
ἀβασάνιστα: 'not to be examined, not to be put to the test'; Cyril means the things beyond us are not to be probed.
συνέσει ... τιμᾶται λαμπρῶς: dative of means, 'are splendidly honoured by understanding'; the sense is that wise understanding honours such matters by not prying.

κἂν δοῦλος κἂν ἐλεύθερος: possible echo of Galatians 3:28 or Colossians 3:11; left uncited in the reading text as uncertain. Romans 10:12 ('no distinction between Jew and Greek') stands behind ἀδιαφόρως.
ἄρτι μὲν γὰρ ὡς ἀπειθῆ κατῃτιᾶτο: refers back to Paul's charge in Romans 10:21 ('a disobedient and contrary people'); a possible reference, not cited inline.

περισαίνοντος ... θωπικῶς ὑποτρέχοντος: literally 'fawning upon ... flatteringly running up to'; Cyril uses the words in praise of Paul's tact, rendered 'gently wins over ... coming round them with coaxing words'.
ἱερουργός: echoes Romans 15:16 (ἱερουργοῦντα τὸ εὐαγγέλιον); possible, noted only.
πεπαροίνηκεν ἐφ' ἑαυτῷ: 'has behaved outrageously (as in drunken violence) against himself'; rendered 'has acted outrageously, to its own harm'.
Israel is treated as a singular collective in the Greek; English uses 'it', and 'them' where Cyril shifts to τὸν λαόν.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos u09 rem close
